# 12-Week Postpartum Return-to-Movement Programme

### Client Profile
**Age:** 33 | **Status:** 4 weeks post uncomplicated C-section | **Clearance:** Light activity only until 6-week OB check | **Equipment:** Yoga mat, home setting | **Goal:** Safe, progressive return to functional movement and core integrity

---

## Important Clinical Notes for the Trainer

Before beginning, please review these non-negotiables with your client and keep them front of mind throughout every session.

**C-section specific considerations:** The abdominal wall has been cut through multiple layers — skin, fascia, and uterus. Even with OB clearance at six weeks, internal healing continues for up to twelve months. The scar tissue needs time and gentle mobilisation before loading. Watch for any pulling, tugging, or sharp sensation at the scar site and treat it as a stop signal.

**Diastasis Recti (DR) awareness:** Virtually all pregnant women have some degree of abdominal separation. Before progressing any core work, assess for DR at the six-week check or refer to a pelvic floor physiotherapist. Coning or doming at the midline during any exercise is a red flag — regress immediately.

**Pelvic floor first:** The pelvic floor is the foundation of the entire programme. Leaking, heaviness, pressure, or pain in the pelvic region at any point means the load is too high. A referral to a Women's Health Physiotherapist is strongly recommended before or alongside this programme, and is considered best practice.

**Red flags — stop and seek medical advice if she experiences:** Increased lochia (bleeding), pain at the incision site, pelvic heaviness or prolapse symptoms, urinary or faecal leakage, dizziness, or chest pain.

---

## Programme Overview

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1: Breathe & Reconnect | 1–2 (Programme Weeks 1–2, Client Weeks 4–6 postpartum) | Diaphragmatic breathing, pelvic floor awareness, gentle mobility |
| Phase 2: Foundation | 3–5 (Post 6-week OB clearance) | Core canister activation, scar mobilisation, postural work |
| Phase 3: Integration | 6–9 | Full-body functional movement, progressive loading with bodyweight |
| Phase 4: Strength & Resilience | 10–12 | Compound patterns, endurance, return to higher-demand activity |

**Session frequency:** 4–5 sessions per week in Phases 1–2 (short, 15–20 minutes), building to 3–4 sessions of 30–45 minutes in Phases 3–4, plus daily walking targets.

---

## PHASE 1: BREATHE & RECONNECT
### Weeks 1–2 of Programme (Client is 4–6 weeks postpartum)

**Phase Goal:** Restore the connection between breath, pelvic floor, and deep abdominals. No loading of the abdominal wall. No exercises that increase intra-abdominal pressure. This phase is entirely about neurological reconnection, not fitness.

**Walking target:** Begin with 5–10 minutes of gentle walking daily, adding 2–3 minutes every 2–3 days as comfort allows. Stop if there is any pulling at the scar or pelvic heaviness.

---

### Week 1

**Session structure:** Daily, 15 minutes. All exercises are performed lying down or in a supported position.

**Session A — Breath & Pelvic Floor Awareness**

*Diaphragmatic Breathing (360° Breathing)*
Lie on the back with knees bent, feet flat, a pillow under the head if needed. Place one hand on the chest and one on the lower ribcage. Inhale slowly through the nose for 4 counts, feeling the ribcage expand in all directions — front, sides, and back into the mat. The belly rises gently. Exhale slowly through pursed lips or a gentle "shhh" for 6–8 counts, feeling the ribcage drop and the belly soften. Perform 10 breaths. Rest 1 minute. Repeat for 3 sets. This is the single most important exercise in the entire programme. Everything else is built on top of it.

*Pelvic Floor Awareness — "Elevator" Technique*
Remaining in the same position, on the exhale, gently imagine lifting a blueberry with the pelvic floor — a subtle lift and squeeze, not a grip. Hold for 3–5 seconds, then fully release and let go completely on the inhale. The release is as important as the lift. Perform 8–10 repetitions. Rest 1 minute. Repeat for 2 sets. Cue her to avoid holding her breath, gripping her glutes, or bracing her abdomen.

*Gentle Ankle Circles and Foot Pumps*
Still lying down, extend one leg at a time and perform 10 slow ankle circles in each direction, then 10 foot pumps (flex and point). This supports circulation and is particularly relevant post-surgery. Perform on both feet.

*Supported Thoracic Rotation (Supine)*
Lying on the back, knees bent and together, arms out to the sides in a T-shape. On the exhale, very slowly let both knees drift 2–3 inches to the right, feeling a gentle rotation through the mid-back. Inhale to return. Exhale to the left. The movement is tiny — this is not a full windshield wiper. Perform 5 repetitions each side for 2 sets. Stop if there is any pulling at the scar.

**Session B — Gentle Mobility (alternate with Session A or perform on separate days)**

*Neck Rolls and Shoulder Circles*
Seated or lying, perform 5 slow half-circles of the neck each direction, then 10 backward shoulder rolls. Postpartum posture is typically rounded forward from feeding and carrying, so backward movement is prioritised.

*Cat-Cow (Modified — Breath-Led Only)*
On hands and knees, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. This position should feel comfortable — place a folded blanket under the knees if needed. On the inhale, allow the belly to gently drop toward the mat and the gaze to soften forward (cow). On the exhale, gently round the upper back toward the ceiling, tucking the chin (cat). The movement is led entirely by the breath and is very small. There is no active abdominal contraction. Perform 8 repetitions for 2 sets. If the wrist position is uncomfortable, perform on fists or forearms.

*Child's Pose (Modified)*
From hands and knees, sit back toward the heels — only as far as is comfortable given the scar. Arms extended forward or resting alongside the body. Hold for 5 slow breaths. This gently decompresses the lumbar spine and provides a moment of rest.

*Glute Bridge — Breath-Led, Minimal Load*
Lying on the back, knees bent, feet hip-width apart. On the exhale, gently engage the pelvic floor (the elevator lift), then slowly peel the hips off the mat just 2–3 inches — this is not a full bridge. Hold for 2 breaths, then slowly lower on the inhale. The goal is not glute strength at this stage; it is practising the exhale-lift-move sequence. Perform 8 repetitions for 2 sets. If there is any pulling at the scar, reduce the range further or omit entirely this week.

---

### Week 2

**Progression:** Slightly increase breath hold times and pelvic floor hold duration. Begin to add very gentle lower limb movement.

**Daily sessions remain 15–20 minutes. Walking increases to 10–15 minutes daily.**

*Diaphragmatic Breathing:* Continue as Week 1. Begin to add a gentle pelvic floor lift on every exhale as a habit, not a separate exercise — this is called the "breathing and bracing" pattern and will underpin all future exercise.

*Pelvic Floor — Long Holds and Quick Flicks*
Add a second variation: after the elevator holds, perform 10 quick, sharp contractions — lift and release rapidly. These target the fast-twitch pelvic floor fibres responsible for cough and sneeze responses. Perform 2 sets of 10 quick flicks after the slow holds.

*Heel Slides*
Lying on the back, knees bent. On the exhale with a gentle pelvic floor lift, slowly slide one heel along the mat until the leg is nearly straight, then slide it back on the inhale. The lower back should remain in neutral — not arching away from the mat. Perform 8 repetitions each leg for 2 sets. This is the first gentle challenge to the deep abdominal system.

*Glute Bridge — Full Range*
Progress to a full glute bridge this week if the scar is comfortable. Exhale, lift the pelvic floor, then peel the spine off the mat vertebra by vertebra until the hips are in line with the knees and shoulders. Hold for 3 breaths at the top, then lower slowly. Perform 10 repetitions for 3 sets.

*Seated Posture Work*
Sitting cross-legged or in a chair, practise finding a neutral spine — not slumped, not over-arched. Perform 10 gentle shoulder blade squeezes, holding 3 seconds each. Follow with 10 chin tucks (drawing the chin straight back to create a "double chin" — this corrects forward head posture common in new mothers).

*Continue all mobility work from Week 1.*

---

**End of Phase 1 — Six-Week OB Check**

Before proceeding to Phase 2, confirm the following with the client:

- OB has given clearance to progress activity
- No ongoing bleeding, pain, or infection at the scar site
- Pelvic floor symptoms (if any) have been discussed with a healthcare provider
- Ideally, a pelvic floor physiotherapy assessment has been completed or is booked

If clearance is not given, remain in Phase 1 until it is. There is no rush.

---

## PHASE 2: FOUNDATION
### Weeks 3–5 of Programme (Client is 6–9 weeks postpartum)

**Phase Goal:** Establish the core canister — the coordinated function of the diaphragm, pelvic floor, deep abdominals (transversus abdominis), and multifidus. Begin gentle scar tissue mobilisation. Introduce postural loading and hip stability work. Sessions increase to 20–25 minutes, 4–5 times per week.

**Walking target:** Build to 20–30 minutes daily at a comfortable pace. Introduce gentle hills only if there is no pelvic heaviness.

**Scar Mobilisation Note:** From approximately 6–8 weeks, once the scar is fully closed and there is no scabbing, gentle scar massage can begin. Instruct the client to use clean fingertips to gently move the skin around the scar in small circles, then horizontally and vertically — not on the scar itself initially, but around it. This prevents adhesions and improves tissue mobility. Begin with 2–3 minutes daily and progress to direct scar massage as sensitivity allows. If she is unsure, a pelvic floor physiotherapist can guide this.

---

### Week 3

**Session A — Core Canister Activation (4 sessions this week)**

*Diaphragmatic Breathing with Active Pelvic Floor:* Now a warm-up ritual for every session. 10 breaths, 2 sets.

*Dead Bug — Modified (No Leg Extension)*
Lying on the back, arms reaching toward the ceiling, knees bent at 90 degrees in the air (tabletop position). On the exhale with a pelvic floor lift, slowly lower one foot toward the mat — keeping the knee bent — until the foot hovers 2–3 inches above the mat. Inhale to return. Alternate sides. The lower back must stay in contact with the mat throughout. If the back arches, the range is too large. Perform 6 repetitions each side for 3 sets. Watch carefully for doming or coning at the midline — if present, regress to heel slides.

*Glute Bridge with Hold:* 10 repetitions, 3 sets, holding 5 seconds at the top. Add a gentle pelvic floor squeeze at the top of each rep.

*Clamshell*
Lying on the side, hips stacked, knees bent at 45 degrees, feet together. On the exhale, rotate the top knee toward the ceiling like a clamshell opening, keeping the feet together and the pelvis still. Lower slowly. Perform 12 repetitions each side for 3 sets. Place a hand on the hip to ensure the pelvis is not rocking backward. This targets the hip abductors and external rotators, which are critical for pelvic stability.

*Bird Dog — Modified (Arm Only)*
On hands and knees in the neutral spine position. On the exhale with a pelvic floor lift, slowly extend one arm forward to shoulder height. Hold for 3 breaths, then lower on the inhale. Alternate sides. Perform 8 repetitions each side for 2 sets. The spine must not rotate or shift. Begin with arm only before adding leg.

---

### Week 4

**Progression:** Add leg component to Bird Dog. Increase Dead Bug range. Introduce standing work.

*Dead Bug — Full Extension (if no doming)*
From the same starting position, on the exhale, simultaneously lower the opposite arm overhead and extend the opposite leg toward the mat, hovering both 2–3 inches above the mat. Inhale to return. Perform 6 repetitions each side for 3 sets. This is a significant progression — only advance if Week 3 was symptom-free.

*Bird Dog — Full (Arm and Opposite Leg)*
On the exhale, extend the right arm and left leg simultaneously, holding for 3 breaths. The hips must remain level — place a water bottle on the lower back as a feedback tool if helpful. Perform 8 repetitions each side for 3 sets.

*Standing Hip Hinge Introduction*
Standing with feet hip-width apart, hands on hips. On the exhale, hinge forward from the hips — not the waist — pushing the hips back as if closing a car door with them, maintaining a long neutral spine. Hinge to approximately 45 degrees, then drive the hips forward to return to standing. Perform 10 repetitions for 3 sets. This is the foundation of every deadlift and forward-bending movement she will ever do.

*Wall Sit — Isometric Hold*
Standing with the back against a wall, slide down until the thighs are at approximately 45 degrees (not a full 90-degree squat yet). Hold for 10–15 seconds, breathing normally with a gentle pelvic floor engagement. Perform 3 holds. This introduces lower limb loading without impact.

*Side-Lying Hip Abduction*
Lying on the side, bottom knee slightly bent for stability, top leg straight. On the exhale, lift the top leg to hip height — no higher. Lower slowly. Perform 12 repetitions each side for 3 sets. Progress from clamshell to this movement.

---

### Week 5

**Progression:** Introduce bodyweight squat pattern, increase endurance of holds, add upper body work.

*Bodyweight Squat — Assisted*
Standing facing a wall or holding a door frame for balance. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. On the inhale, sit back and down as if toward a chair, keeping the chest tall and knees tracking over the toes. Lower to a comfortable depth — initially this may be only 30–40 degrees. On the exhale with a pelvic floor lift, drive through the heels to stand. Perform 10 repetitions for 3 sets. The exhale on the effort (the standing phase) is critical — this is the intra-abdominal pressure management strategy she will use for all loaded movements.

*Wall Push-Up*
Standing facing a wall, hands at shoulder height and width. On the inhale, lower the chest toward the wall. On the exhale, push away. Perform 10 repetitions for 3 sets. This reintroduces upper body pressing without loading the abdominal wall in a way that a floor push-up would.

*Glute Bridge — Single Leg (Supported)*
From the standard bridge position, extend one leg straight while keeping the hips level. Perform the bridge on the single supporting leg. Perform 8 repetitions each side for 3 sets. This is a significant progression — only add if the bilateral bridge is strong and symptom-free.

*Continue Dead Bug, Bird Dog, and Hip Hinge from Week 4.*

**Session frequency this week:** 4 sessions, each 25–30 minutes.

---

## PHASE 3: INTEGRATION
### Weeks 6–9 of Programme (Client is 10–13 weeks postpartum)

**Phase Goal:** Integrate the core canister into full-body functional movement patterns. Introduce all major movement patterns — squat, hinge, push, pull, carry — using bodyweight. Sessions are 30–40 minutes, 3–4 times per week, with active recovery days.

**Walking target:** 30–45 minutes daily. Begin to introduce brisker pace intervals — 1 minute faster, 2 minutes normal — if pelvic floor is symptom-free.

**Session Structure from Phase 3 onward:**
Each session follows this format:
- **Warm-up (5 minutes):** Diaphragmatic breathing (5 breaths), pelvic floor activation, cat-cow, hip circles, thoracic rotation
- **Main work (20–30 minutes):** As prescribed below
- **Cool-down (5 minutes):** Child's pose, supine spinal twist, hip flexor stretch, diaphragmatic breathing to close

---

### Week 6

**Session A — Lower Body Focus**

| Exercise | Sets | Reps/Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bodyweight Squat | 3 | 12 | Exhale on the way up |
| Romanian Deadlift (bodyweight) | 3 | 10 | Hip hinge pattern, long spine |
| Glute Bridge | 3 | 12, 5-sec hold | Pelvic floor squeeze at top |
| Clamshell | 3 | 15 each side | Controlled tempo |
| Side-Lying Hip Abduction | 3 | 12 each side | |

**Session B — Upper Body and Core**

| Exercise | Sets | Reps/Duration | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wall Push-Up | 3 | 12 | Progress to incline if easy |
| Bird Dog | 3 | 8 each side | 3-sec hold at top |
| Dead Bug | 3 | 6 each side | Full extension |
| Seated Row (resistance band or towel around door handle) | 3 | 12 | Retract shoulder blades |
| Prone Cobra | 3 | 8, 3-sec hold | Gentle back extension, hands by shoulders |

**Session C — Full Body Circuit (2 rounds, rest 90 seconds between rounds)**

Bodyweight Squat × 10, Wall Push-Up × 10, Hip Hinge × 10, Bird Dog × 6 each side, Glute Bridge × 10, Clamshell × 10 each side.

**Session D — Active Recovery**
30-minute walk. Gentle yoga-style stretching: hip flexor stretch in kneeling lunge, seated hamstring stretch, thoracic rotation seated, child's pose. 10 minutes of pelvic floor work.

---

### Week 7

**Progression:** Increase squat depth, introduce step-up, add incline push-up.

*Squat:* Aim for thighs approaching parallel. Add a 2-second pause at the bottom. 3 sets of 12.

*Step-Up (onto a low step, stair, or thick book stack — approximately 15–20cm)*
Standing facing the step. Place the right foot on the step, drive through the heel to step up, bringing the left foot to meet it. Step down with control. Perform 10 repetitions each leg for 3 sets. This is a significant functional movement for a new mother — getting up from the floor, climbing stairs with a baby. Ensure the knee tracks over the toes and the pelvis does not drop to the side.

*Incline Push-Up:*
Hands on a sturdy chair seat or low bench rather than the wall. This increases the load compared to the wall push-up. 3 sets of 10.

*Reverse Lunge Introduction:*
Standing, step one foot back and lower the back knee toward the mat — only as far as is comfortable. The front shin should remain vertical. Drive through the front heel to return. Perform 8 repetitions each leg for 3 sets. The reverse lunge is preferred over the forward lunge at this stage as it places less stress on the pelvic floor.

*Continue all core work from Week 6.*

---

### Week 8

**Progression:** Introduce lateral movement, increase volume slightly, add a balance challenge.

*Lateral Squat Walk:*
Place a resistance band just above the knees if available — if not, perform without. In a quarter-squat position, step sideways 10 steps to the right, then 10 steps to the left. Perform 3 sets. This targets the hip abductors in a functional, standing position.

*Single-Leg Deadlift (Supported):*
Standing on one leg, holding a wall for balance. Hinge forward from the hip, extending the free leg behind for counterbalance, until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Return to standing. Perform 8 repetitions each side for 3 sets. This challenges balance, hip stability, and the posterior chain.

*Plank — Modified (Forearm, Knees Down):*
This is the first plank introduction. Forearms on the mat, knees down, body in a straight line from knees to shoulders. On the exhale, engage the pelvic floor and gently draw the lower belly in — not a hard brace, a gentle lift. Hold for 10–15 seconds. Perform 3 holds. Watch carefully for doming at the midline, breath-holding, or any pelvic floor symptoms. If any are present, return to Dead Bug and Bird Dog only.

*Push-Up — Incline, Increased Range:* 3 sets of 12.

---

### Week 9

**Progression:** Consolidation week. Increase repetitions and sets on established exercises rather than introducing new movements. Focus on quality, tempo, and breathing mechanics.

*Squat:* 4 sets of 15. Add a 3-second lowering phase.
*Reverse Lunge:* 3 sets of 10 each leg.
*Single-Leg Deadlift:* 3 sets of 10 each leg, reduce wall support if balance allows.
*Forearm Plank (Knees):* Build to 3 × 20–25 seconds.
*Incline Push-Up:* 3 sets of 15.
*Bird Dog:* 3 sets of 10 each side, 5-second hold.
*Glute Bridge — Single Leg:* 3 sets of 10 each side.

**By the end of Week 9, the client should feel strong, stable, and confident in all fundamental movement patterns. She should have no pelvic floor symptoms during exercise. If she does, revisit Phase 2 work and consider pelvic floor physiotherapy before proceeding.**

### Weeks 10–12 of Programme (Client is 14–16 weeks postpartum)

**Phase Goal:** Build genuine strength and endurance through progressive bodyweight loading. Introduce full push-up, full plank, and more demanding compound movements. Prepare the client for a return to higher-impact activity (running, HIIT) if desired — though impact return is typically not recommended until at least 12 weeks postpartum and ideally after pelvic floor physiotherapy clearance.

**Session frequency:** 3–4 sessions per week, 40–45 minutes each.

**Walking target:** 45–60 minutes daily or equivalent. Introduce jogging intervals only if pelvic floor physiotherapy has cleared her and there are zero symptoms — this is a clinical decision, not a fitness one.

# Nutrition Plan: Postpartum & Breastfeeding Support
### Integrated with 12-Week Return-to-Movement Programme

---

## Important Framing Note for the Trainer

Before presenting any nutrition guidance to this client, establish her relationship with food and body image. The postpartum period carries significant risk for disordered eating — pressure to "get your body back" is pervasive and harmful. The language used throughout this plan is deliberately performance- and nourishment-focused, not weight-loss focused. **Weight loss is not a goal of this programme.** Fat loss, if it occurs, will be a byproduct of nourishing movement and adequate fuelling — never a target to chase while breastfeeding. If at any point the client expresses restrictive behaviours, obsessive calorie counting, or significant body image distress, refer to a registered dietitian and/or mental health professional.

Additionally, you are a personal trainer, not a registered dietitian. This plan provides evidence-informed general guidance. For any client with specific medical needs — gestational diabetes history, thyroid conditions, anaemia, food allergies, or disordered eating history — refer to a registered dietitian or her GP.

---

## Breastfeeding Nutrition: The Physiological Reality

Breastfeeding is one of the most metabolically demanding things the human body does. Understanding the numbers helps frame every recommendation that follows.

**Breast milk production costs approximately 400–500 calories per day.** The body is remarkably efficient at prioritising milk supply — it will draw from maternal stores if intake is insufficient, which means the mother pays the price in energy, bone density, hormonal balance, and recovery capacity, not the baby. This is why restriction is genuinely dangerous in this context, not just inadvisable.

**Exclusive breastfeeding recommendations** from major health bodies (NHS, WHO, Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics) suggest an additional 300–500 calories per day above pre-pregnancy maintenance needs, depending on the degree to which body stores are contributing. A woman who is exclusively breastfeeding, healing from major abdominal surgery, sleep-deprived, and beginning an exercise programme has extraordinarily high nutritional demands. Undereating will compromise all four simultaneously.

**Key nutrients with elevated requirements during breastfeeding:**

| Nutrient | Why It Matters Postpartum | Key Sources |
|---|---|---|
| Calories | Milk production, surgical healing, energy for movement | Whole foods across all macronutrients |
| Protein | Tissue repair (C-section), muscle recovery, milk protein content | Meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes, tofu |
| Iron | Blood loss from surgery, fatigue, oxygen transport | Red meat, lentils, spinach, fortified cereals |
| Calcium | Bone density (drawn upon during lactation), muscle function | Dairy, fortified plant milks, sardines, leafy greens |
| Vitamin D | Calcium absorption, immune function, mood | Oily fish, eggs, fortified foods, sunlight, supplement |
| Omega-3 (DHA) | Infant brain development, maternal mood, inflammation | Oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed, algae-based supplement |
| Iodine | Infant thyroid and brain development | Dairy, fish, eggs, iodised salt |
| Choline | Infant brain development, liver function | Eggs, meat, fish, legumes |
| Folate | Continued cellular repair and infant development | Leafy greens, legumes, fortified foods |
| Vitamin B12 | Energy, nerve function, infant neurological development | Meat, fish, dairy, eggs (supplement if plant-based) |
| Zinc | Wound healing post C-section, immune function | Meat, shellfish, seeds, legumes |
| Magnesium | Sleep quality, muscle recovery, mood regulation | Nuts, seeds, dark chocolate, leafy greens, wholegrains |
| Fluids | Milk production, circulation, recovery | Water, milk, herbal teas, food water content |

---

## Calorie and Macronutrient Framework

Rather than prescribing rigid calorie targets — which are impractical for a sleep-deprived new mother and can foster an unhealthy relationship with food — this plan uses a **structured eating pattern** approach. The goal is to ensure she eats enough, often enough, with the right nutritional density, without requiring her to weigh food or track apps during one of the most demanding periods of her life.

### Estimated Daily Calorie Range

For a 33-year-old woman of average height and weight, lightly active and exclusively breastfeeding:

**Approximate daily need: 2,200–2,500 calories**

This will increase slightly as exercise volume increases in Phases 3 and 4. The emphasis is always on eating to hunger and energy cues rather than hitting a number. If she is consistently exhausted beyond normal new-parent tiredness, losing weight rapidly, or noticing a drop in milk supply, these are signs she is undereating and intake should increase.

### Macronutrient Targets (Approximate)

| Macronutrient | Daily Target | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Protein | 1.6–2.0g per kg bodyweight | Elevated for surgical healing and muscle recovery; supports satiety |
| Carbohydrates | 45–55% of total calories | Primary fuel for brain, milk production, and exercise; do not restrict |
| Fat | 25–35% of total calories | Essential for fat-soluble vitamins, hormone production, and infant brain development |

**For a 70kg woman as an example:**
- Protein: 112–140g per day
- Carbohydrates: approximately 250–340g per day
- Fat: approximately 60–95g per day

Carbohydrates are specifically highlighted because they are frequently and wrongly restricted postpartum. Glucose is the primary fuel for milk production and for the recovering brain. Low-carbohydrate diets are contraindicated during breastfeeding.

---

## Hydration

Breast milk is approximately 87% water. Dehydration directly reduces milk volume and quality, impairs physical performance, slows wound healing, and worsens fatigue and mood.

**Daily fluid target: 2.5–3.5 litres**, increasing toward the higher end on exercise days and in warm weather.

**Practical strategy:** Keep a large water bottle (750ml–1 litre) at every feeding station. Drink a full glass of water every time she sits down to breastfeed — this creates a reliable habit and ensures she is drinking at least 6–8 times per day around feeds alone. Herbal teas (peppermint, ginger, chamomile, rooibos) count toward fluid intake and can be warming and comforting. Limit caffeine to 200mg per day maximum (approximately 1–2 cups of coffee or 3–4 cups of tea) — caffeine passes into breast milk and can affect infant sleep.

**Signs of dehydration to watch for:** Dark urine, headaches, reduced milk supply, dizziness during exercise, constipation.

---

## Meal Structure: The Postpartum Plate

Given the reality of life with a newborn — unpredictable schedules, one-handed eating, interrupted meals, exhaustion — the meal structure must be realistic above all else. The framework below is built around simplicity, batch cooking, and nutrient density per bite.

### The Three-Tier Approach

**Tier 1 — Non-Negotiable Anchors (3 main meals)**
These are the structural meals of the day. Each should contain protein, complex carbohydrate, healthy fat, and vegetables or fruit. They do not need to be elaborate. A bowl of porridge with eggs on the side is a complete anchor meal.

**Tier 2 — Planned Snacks (2–3 per day)**
Snacks are not optional extras — they are essential given the caloric demands of breastfeeding and recovery. Each snack should contain at least one protein source to support satiety and tissue repair.

**Tier 3 — Opportunistic Eating**
This is the reality of new parenthood. A handful of nuts grabbed between feeds, a banana eaten standing at the kitchen counter, a slice of toast at 3am. These moments matter and should be supported with accessible, nutritious options kept within easy reach. The goal is never perfection — it is consistent adequacy.

---

## Phase-by-Phase Nutrition Guidance

### Phase 1 Nutrition (Programme Weeks 1–2 | 4–6 Weeks Postpartum)

**Priority:** Healing, milk establishment, energy restoration. Exercise demands are minimal, so the nutritional focus is entirely on recovery and lactation support.

**Key focus areas this phase:**

*Protein for wound healing.* The C-section incision requires significant protein for collagen synthesis and tissue repair. Aim for a protein source at every single meal and snack without exception. If appetite is poor — which is common in the early weeks due to hormonal shifts and exhaustion — prioritise protein above all other macronutrients.

*Iron replenishment.* Surgical blood loss depletes iron stores. Fatigue that goes beyond normal new-parent tiredness may indicate low iron. Include red meat 2–3 times per week, or plant-based iron sources (lentils, spinach, fortified cereals) paired with vitamin C to enhance absorption. Avoid tea or coffee within an hour of iron-rich meals as tannins inhibit absorption.

*Fibre and gut health.* Constipation is extremely common post-C-section due to anaesthesia, pain medication, reduced mobility, and dehydration. Prioritise fibre-rich foods — oats, lentils, vegetables, fruit, wholegrains — alongside adequate hydration. If constipation is severe, discuss with her GP or midwife.

*Anti-inflammatory foods.* The body is in an active healing state. Foods rich in omega-3 fatty acids (oily fish, walnuts, flaxseed), antioxidants (berries, leafy greens, colourful vegetables), and polyphenols (olive oil, green tea, dark chocolate) support the healing process and may reduce scar tissue formation.

**Sample Day — Phase 1**

*On waking (before or during first feed):*
Large glass of water. A small snack if hungry — a banana and a handful of almonds, or a piece of toast with peanut butter.

*Breakfast:*
Porridge made with whole milk or fortified oat milk, topped with a tablespoon of ground flaxseed, a handful of berries, and a drizzle of honey. Two scrambled eggs on the side, or stirred through the oats for a savoury version. This meal delivers complex carbohydrates, protein, omega-3s, iron, and calcium in one bowl.

*Mid-morning snack:*
Full-fat Greek yoghurt with a handful of mixed seeds and a piece of fruit. Greek yoghurt is one of the most nutrient-dense, easy-to-eat postpartum foods — high in protein, calcium, iodine, and probiotics.

*Lunch:*
A large bowl of lentil soup (batch-cooked and frozen in portions before birth if possible, or a good-quality shop-bought version) with a thick slice of wholegrain bread and butter. A small side salad with olive oil dressing. Lentils provide protein, iron, folate, and fibre in a warm, easy-to-eat format.

*Afternoon snack:*
Oatcakes with hummus and sliced cucumber, or a small handful of mixed nuts and dried fruit. Keep this within arm's reach of the feeding chair.

*Dinner:*
Salmon fillet (baked or pan-fried — minimal effort) with sweet potato mash and steamed broccoli. Salmon provides DHA, protein, vitamin D, and iodine. Sweet potato provides complex carbohydrates, beta-carotene, and potassium. Broccoli provides folate, vitamin C, and calcium.

*Evening snack (important — do not skip):*
Warm whole milk with a teaspoon of honey, or a small bowl of cereal with milk, or toast with nut butter. An evening snack supports overnight milk production and prevents the blood sugar dip that worsens night-feed exhaustion.

**Approximate nutritional profile of this sample day:** ~2,300 calories, ~130g protein, ~270g carbohydrates, ~85g fat.

---

### Phase 2 Nutrition (Programme Weeks 3–5 | 6–9 Weeks Postpartum)

**Priority:** Continue healing support, begin fuelling light exercise, establish sustainable eating habits.

As exercise begins in earnest, the timing of food around sessions becomes relevant for the first time. However, given that Phase 2 sessions are short (20–25 minutes) and low intensity, pre- and post-workout nutrition does not need to be complicated.

**Pre-exercise (30–60 minutes before session):**
A small, easily digestible snack containing carbohydrates and a little protein. Examples: a banana with a tablespoon of nut butter, a small pot of yoghurt with fruit, a slice of toast with honey. Avoid high-fat or high-fibre foods immediately before exercise as they slow digestion and can cause discomfort.

**Post-exercise:**
Eat a full meal or substantial snack within 60–90 minutes of finishing. This does not need to be a protein shake — a normal balanced meal is ideal. The post-exercise window supports muscle repair and glycogen replenishment.

**New focus this phase — Calcium and Bone Health:**
Lactation draws calcium from maternal bone stores. This is a normal physiological process, but adequate dietary calcium minimises bone density loss. Aim for 3–4 servings of calcium-rich foods daily. One serving equals: a glass of milk, a pot of yoghurt, a matchbox-sized piece of cheese, a tin of sardines with bones, or a large serving of fortified plant milk. If dairy-free, calcium-set tofu, fortified oat milk, and leafy greens (kale, bok choy, broccoli) are good sources, but a calcium supplement may be warranted — discuss with her GP.

**New focus this phase — Vitamin D:**
The UK government recommends all adults supplement with 10 micrograms (400 IU) of vitamin D daily, year-round. For a breastfeeding woman, this is particularly important as breast milk is naturally low in vitamin D. Many practitioners recommend 1,000–2,000 IU daily for breastfeeding mothers, but advise her to discuss the specific dose with her GP or midwife.

**Sample additions and swaps for Phase 2:**

Introduce more variety now that the acute recovery phase is passing and appetite is likely improving. Add more colour to meals — aim for five different coloured vegetables or fruits per day as a simple visual target. Begin batch cooking on less exhausted days: a large pot of soup, a tray of roasted vegetables, a batch of energy balls, hard-boiled eggs in the fridge. These become the building blocks of easy, nutritious meals throughout the week.

---

### Phase 3 Nutrition (Programme Weeks 6–9 | 10–13 Weeks Postpartum)

**Priority:** Fuel increasing exercise demands, support muscle development, maintain milk supply, sustain energy across longer and more demanding sessions.

As sessions increase to 30–40 minutes and movement patterns become more demanding, nutritional support for exercise becomes more important.

**Increase total intake slightly** — approximately 100–200 additional calories on training days, coming primarily from carbohydrates and protein. This does not require tracking; it simply means eating a slightly larger post-workout meal or adding an extra snack on training days.

**Pre-workout meal (1–2 hours before a 30–40 minute session):**
A balanced meal containing complex carbohydrates and moderate protein. Examples: porridge with milk and fruit, a wholegrain wrap with chicken and salad, rice cakes with cottage cheese and tomato. Avoid training on an empty stomach — blood sugar management is already challenged by sleep deprivation and breastfeeding.

**Post-workout nutrition (within 60 minutes):**
Aim for 25–35g of protein alongside carbohydrates. Examples: two eggs on wholegrain toast with avocado, a large Greek yoghurt with granola and fruit, a chicken and rice bowl, a smoothie made with milk, banana, oats, and a scoop of protein powder if convenient. The protein target is specific here because Phase 3 introduces genuine muscle-building stimulus for the first time.

**Protein distribution matters.** Research consistently shows that spreading protein across 4–5 eating occasions is more effective for muscle protein synthesis than consuming the same total amount in one or two large meals. Aim for 25–35g of protein at each main meal and 10–20g at each snack.

**Sample High-Protein Day — Phase 3**

| Meal | Food | Approx. Protein |
|---|---|---|
| Breakfast | 3-egg omelette with cheese and spinach, 2 slices wholegrain toast | 35g |
| Mid-morning snack | Greek yoghurt (200g) with mixed seeds | 20g |
| Lunch | Large chicken and quinoa salad with roasted vegetables and olive oil | 40g |
| Pre-workout snack | Banana and 2 tbsp peanut butter | 8g |
| Post-workout | Cottage cheese on rice cakes with cucumber | 20g |
| Dinner | Baked cod with lentils and roasted sweet potato | 40g |
| Evening snack | Warm milk and oatcakes with nut butter | 12g |
| **Total** | | **~175g** |

This sample day provides approximately 2,400 calories and meets the upper end of the protein target for a 70–85kg breastfeeding woman in active recovery.

---

### Phase 4 Nutrition (Programme Weeks 10–12 | 14–16 Weeks Postpartum)

**Priority:** Support peak programme demands, consolidate healthy eating habits for the long term, begin transitioning toward a sustainable post-programme eating pattern.

By this phase, the client is performing genuine strength work and longer walking sessions. Energy demands are at their highest point in the programme. This is not the time to reduce intake — if anything, appetite will be higher and should be honoured.

**Performance nutrition habits to establish:**

*Consistent meal timing.* Aim to eat every 3–4 hours. This supports stable blood sugar, consistent milk supply, sustained energy for exercise, and better mood regulation — all of which are challenged by sleep deprivation.

*Carbohydrate timing around sessions.* On training days, ensure a carbohydrate-containing meal or snack in the 1–2 hours before exercise and again within 60 minutes after. On rest days, carbohydrate intake can be slightly lower but should never be restricted — milk production requires glucose around the clock.

*Prioritise food quality without rigidity.* By Week 10, the goal is for healthy eating to feel habitual rather than effortful. If she is eating predominantly whole foods, hitting her protein targets, staying hydrated, and not restricting, she is doing everything right. Occasional takeaways, birthday cake, and chocolate at 2am are not problems — they are part of a sustainable relationship with food.

**Foods to emphasise in Phase 4:**

*Oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout):* 2–3 portions per week for DHA, protein, vitamin D, and iodine. If she dislikes fish, an algae-based DHA supplement is the most effective alternative.

*Eggs:* Daily if possible. One of the most complete nutritional packages available — protein, choline, vitamin D, B12, iodine, and healthy fat in one affordable, quick-to-prepare food.

*Legumes (lentils, chickpeas, black beans, edamame):* 3–4 times per week. Provide protein, iron, folate, fibre, and complex carbohydrates. Extremely versatile and batch-cook well.

*Leafy greens (spinach, kale, rocket, watercress):* Daily. Calcium, folate, iron, vitamin K, and antioxidants. Add to smoothies, eggs, soups, and pasta for easy inclusion.

*Wholegrains (oats, brown rice, quinoa, wholegrain bread and pasta):* At every main meal. Sustained energy, fibre, B vitamins, and magnesium.

*Nuts and seeds (almonds, walnuts, pumpkin seeds, flaxseed, chia seeds):* Daily as snacks or meal additions. Healthy fats, magnesium, zinc, and protein.

*Full-fat dairy or fortified alternatives:* 3–4 servings daily for calcium, iodine, protein, and fat-soluble vitamins.

*Colourful vegetables and fruit:* Aim for 7–10 portions daily across the full colour spectrum. Each colour represents different phytonutrients and antioxidants that support healing, immunity, and long-term health.

---

## Supplements

The following supplements are generally considered safe and beneficial during breastfeeding. Advise the client to confirm all supplements with her GP or midwife, particularly if she is taking any medications.

| Supplement | Recommended Dose | Rationale | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vitamin D3 | 1,000–2,000 IU daily | UK population is widely deficient; breast milk is low in vitamin D; supports mood, immunity, and bone health | Discuss specific dose with GP; combine with K2 if possible |
| Omega-3 (DHA/EPA) | 200–300mg DHA daily | Infant brain and eye development; maternal mood support; anti-inflammatory | Choose a high-quality fish oil or algae-based supplement (algae is the original source and suitable for vegetarians) |
| Postnatal multivitamin | As directed | Covers iodine, folate, B12, iron, zinc, and other micronutrients; acts as an insurance policy against dietary gaps | Look for a specifically formulated postnatal supplement rather than a standard multivitamin |
| Iron | Only if blood test confirms deficiency | Surgical blood loss increases deficiency risk; do not supplement without testing as excess iron is harmful | GP should test ferritin levels at the 6-week check |
| Magnesium glycinate | 200–400mg before bed | Supports sleep quality, muscle recovery, mood, and constipation | Glycinate form is best absorbed and gentlest on the gut |
| Probiotic | Strain-dependent | Supports gut health post-surgery and antibiotics; may reduce infant colic | Look for Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG or Bifidobacterium strains; discuss with GP |

**What she does not need:** Expensive "milk-boosting" supplements, detox teas, weight-loss supplements, or any product marketed specifically to help her "bounce back." Many of these are unregulated, some contain herbs contraindicated in breastfeeding, and none are necessary.

---

## Practical Strategies for Real Life

### Batch Cooking and Preparation

The single most effective nutrition intervention for a new mother is reducing the friction between hunger and food. Suggest the following weekly preparation habits, ideally done with a partner, family member, or friend:

**Sunday prep session (30–45 minutes):**
- Hard-boil 6–8 eggs and store in the fridge
- Cook a large batch of grains (oats portioned for breakfast, brown rice or quinoa for lunches)
- Roast a large tray of mixed vegetables with olive oil
- Make a large pot of soup or stew and portion into freezer containers
- Wash and chop fruit and vegetables and store in clear containers at eye level in the fridge
- Prepare a batch of energy balls (see recipe below)

**Freezer staples to always have available:**
Frozen edamame, frozen berries, frozen spinach (adds to smoothies and sauces invisibly), frozen fish fillets, frozen peas, pre-portioned smoothie bags, batch-cooked soups and stews.

**One-handed eating options** (for feeding sessions):
Oatcakes with nut butter, energy balls, banana, yoghurt pouch, cheese and crackers, boiled egg, handful of nuts and dried fruit, rice cakes with hummus. Keep a small basket of these options next to the feeding chair.

### Simple Energy Ball Recipe

These are one of the most practical postpartum snacks — no cooking, high in calories and nutrients, one-handed, and genuinely delicious.

**Ingredients:** 200g rolled oats, 4 tablespoons peanut or almond butter, 3 tablespoons honey, 2 tablespoons ground flaxseed, 2 tablespoons chia seeds, 50g dark chocolate chips or dried cranberries, a pinch of salt, 2–3 tablespoons milk to bind if needed.

**Method:** Mix all ingredients together in a bowl. Roll into balls approximately the size of a golf ball. Refrigerate for 30 minutes to firm up. Store in the fridge for up to a week or freeze for up to three months.

**Nutritional profile per ball (approximately):** 150 calories, 5g protein, 15g carbohydrates, 8g fat. Two balls make a substantial snack.

# Phase 4 Expanded & Progressive Strength Programme
### Weeks 10–12 and Beyond: Introducing External Load

---

## Trainer Note on Equipment Progression

The original programme brief specified yoga mat and home setting only. Before introducing any external load, confirm with the client what equipment she has access to or is willing to acquire. The progressions below are structured in tiers so you can apply whichever is available.

**Tier 1 — No equipment:** Bodyweight progressions that dramatically increase mechanical demand through leverage, tempo, and unilateral work. Genuinely challenging and sufficient for meaningful strength development.

**Tier 2 — Resistance bands:** Inexpensive, compact, and highly versatile. A set of three loop bands (light, medium, heavy) and one long resistance band costs approximately £15–25 and transforms the programme. Strongly recommended.

**Tier 3 — Dumbbells or kettlebells:** If the client is willing to invest, a pair of adjustable dumbbells or two kettlebells (8kg and 12kg as a starting pair) opens the full strength programme. This is the ideal progression from Week 10 onward.

**Tier 4 — Gym access:** If she transitions to a gym at any point, notes are included for barbell and cable progressions.

The plan below is written primarily for Tier 2 and 3, with Tier 1 alternatives noted throughout.

---

## Principles of Strength Programming for This Client

Before laying out the sessions, it is worth articulating the specific principles that govern loading decisions for a postpartum client returning to strength work. These are different from standard strength programming principles and must be understood by the trainer.

**Principle 1 — The pelvic floor leads, the load follows.**
Every increase in external load increases intra-abdominal pressure. The pelvic floor must be able to manage that pressure before the load is added. If symptoms appear — leaking, heaviness, pressure, pain — the load is too high regardless of what the programme says. Reduce load, not the exercise.

**Principle 2 — Exhale on effort, always.**
This is the intra-abdominal pressure management strategy that runs through the entire programme. On the hardest part of every repetition — the push, the pull, the stand, the press — she exhales. This coordinates the pelvic floor and deep abdominals with the movement and prevents pressure spikes. It must become automatic before loads become meaningful.

**Principle 3 — Bilateral before unilateral, stable before unstable.**
Progress from two-limb to single-limb movements before adding load. A bilateral squat with 10kg is safer and more productive than a single-leg squat with 5kg at this stage.

**Principle 4 — Posterior chain priority.**
Pregnancy shifts the centre of gravity forward, lengthens and weakens the glutes and hamstrings, and shortens the hip flexors. Postpartum posture is typically anterior pelvic tilt, rounded shoulders, and forward head. The strength programme deliberately emphasises the posterior chain — glutes, hamstrings, back extensors, mid and upper back — to correct these imbalances.

**Principle 5 — Scar tissue and fascial loading.**
The C-section scar involves the linea alba and anterior abdominal fascia. These tissues need progressive tensile loading to remodel properly — but too much too soon creates problems. Loaded carries, deadlifts, and pressing movements all load the anterior abdominal wall. Progress these conservatively and watch for any pulling, tugging, or discomfort at the scar site.

**Principle 6 — Progressive overload applies, but the timeline is longer.**
Standard strength programming might increase load every 1–2 weeks. For this client, every 2–3 weeks is more appropriate, with technique and symptom-free performance as the gating criteria rather than a fixed schedule.

## Strength Programme Structure: Weeks 10–12

### Session Split

From Week 10, the programme moves to a **three-day strength split** with one full-body circuit day and one active recovery day per week.

| Day | Session Type | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 | Lower Body Strength | 40–45 minutes |
| Day 2 | Upper Body Strength | 40–45 minutes |
| Day 3 | Active Recovery | 30–45 minutes walking + mobility |
| Day 4 | Full Body Strength | 40–45 minutes |
| Day 5 | Active Recovery or rest | Walking, stretching, pelvic floor |
| Day 6 | Optional: Full Body Circuit | 30 minutes |
| Day 7 | Rest | |

This split ensures each muscle group receives adequate stimulus and recovery time, while keeping daily session length manageable for a new mother.

## Strength Terminology Used in This Plan

To ensure clarity in the session tables, the following notation is used throughout:

**Sets × Reps** — e.g., 3 × 10 means three sets of ten repetitions.
**Tempo** — written as four digits, e.g., 3-1-2-0. The first number is the eccentric (lowering) phase in seconds, the second is the pause at the bottom, the third is the concentric (lifting) phase, the fourth is the pause at the top. An X in the concentric position means explosive.
**RPE** — Rate of Perceived Exertion on a scale of 1–10. For this programme, working sets should feel like RPE 6–7 in Weeks 10–11, progressing to RPE 7–8 in Week 12. She should never be grinding out reps with compromised form or breath-holding.
**Rest** — Rest periods between sets. Longer rest periods (90–120 seconds) are prescribed for heavier compound movements. Shorter rest (45–60 seconds) for accessory work.

## WEEK 10: LOAD INTRODUCTION

**Theme:** Introduce external load conservatively across all major movement patterns. Establish technique under load before increasing weight. Every session begins with the now-established warm-up ritual and ends with the cool-down sequence.

**Starting loads:** Begin lighter than feels necessary. The first week of loaded work is about neuromuscular patterning, not maximum effort. She should finish each set feeling like she had 3–4 more reps in reserve.

---

### Day 1 — Lower Body Strength

**Warm-Up (5 minutes)**
Diaphragmatic breathing × 10 breaths, pelvic floor activation × 10 slow holds and 10 quick flicks, cat-cow × 10, hip circles × 10 each direction, bodyweight squat × 10 slow, glute bridge × 10.

---

**A1 — Goblet Squat**
*The goblet squat is the ideal first loaded squat for a postpartum client. Holding the weight at the chest acts as a counterbalance, making it easier to maintain an upright torso and neutral spine. It also loads the anterior abdominal wall gently through the isometric hold, which is appropriate at this stage.*

Hold one dumbbell or kettlebell vertically at the chest, elbows pointing down. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. On the inhale, sit back and down into the squat, keeping the chest tall and knees tracking over the toes. Aim for thighs parallel to the floor or as deep as is comfortable and symptom-free. On the exhale, drive through the heels to stand, squeezing the glutes at the top.

**Week 10:** 3 × 10 | Tempo: 3-1-2-0 | Rest: 90 seconds | Load: 6–8kg | RPE: 6

*Tier 1 alternative:* Bodyweight squat with a 4-second lowering phase and 2-second pause at the bottom. 3 × 12.
*Tier 2 alternative:* Loop band just above knees to add hip abductor engagement. Bodyweight or light load.
*Progression trigger:* When 3 × 10 feels like RPE 5 or below with perfect form, increase load by 2kg.

---

**A2 — Romanian Deadlift (RDL)**
*The RDL is the foundational posterior chain exercise and the most important movement in this programme. It directly targets the glutes and hamstrings, which are lengthened and inhibited after pregnancy, and teaches the hip hinge pattern under load. It also loads the erector spinae and, through the grip, the entire posterior chain.*

Hold a dumbbell in each hand (or one kettlebell in both hands) in front of the thighs. Stand with feet hip-width apart, soft bend in the knees. On the inhale, hinge from the hips — pushing them back as if toward a wall behind her — allowing the weights to travel down the front of the thighs. The back remains long and neutral throughout; this is not a forward bend from the waist. Lower until a stretch is felt in the hamstrings — typically when the weights reach mid-shin level. On the exhale, drive the hips forward to return to standing, squeezing the glutes at the top.

**Week 10:** 3 × 10 | Tempo: 3-1-2-1 | Rest: 90 seconds | Load: 6–8kg each hand (or 10–12kg single kettlebell) | RPE: 6–7

*Tier 1 alternative:* Single-leg deadlift with bodyweight, 3 × 8 each side.
*Cue to watch for:* Lower back rounding at the bottom of the movement is the most common error. If this occurs, reduce the range of motion — she does not need to reach the floor. The stretch in the hamstrings, not the position of the weights, determines the endpoint.

---

**B1 — Reverse Lunge with Dumbbells**
*The reverse lunge is preferred over the forward lunge throughout this programme because the deceleration forces are lower, reducing pelvic floor impact. Adding dumbbells held at the sides increases the load through the legs without compressing the spine.*

Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides. Stand tall. Step one foot back and lower the back knee toward the mat in a controlled manner, keeping the front shin vertical and the torso upright. The front thigh should approach parallel to the floor. On the exhale, drive through the front heel to return to standing. Alternate legs.

**Week 10:** 3 × 8 each leg | Tempo: 3-1-2-0 | Rest: 90 seconds | Load: 4–6kg each hand | RPE: 6

*Tier 1 alternative:* Bodyweight reverse lunge with a 4-second lowering phase. 3 × 10 each leg.
*Tier 2 alternative:* Loop band just above knees to add hip abductor challenge.
*Progression note:* Before increasing load, ensure the pelvis is not dropping to the side (Trendelenburg sign) during the movement. If it is, reduce load and add more clamshell and hip abduction work.

---

**B2 — Glute Bridge with Load**
*The loaded glute bridge is a safe and highly effective way to increase posterior chain stimulus without spinal compression. The supine position also means the pelvic floor is in a supported orientation, making it appropriate for early loaded work.*

Lie on the back, knees bent, feet hip-width apart. Place a dumbbell or folded resistance band across the hip crease — not on the abdomen. On the exhale with a pelvic floor lift, drive the hips toward the ceiling, squeezing the glutes hard at the top. Hold for 2 seconds. Lower slowly.

**Week 10:** 3 × 12 | Tempo: 2-2-2-0 | Rest: 60 seconds | Load: 8–12kg dumbbell across hips | RPE: 6–7

*Tier 1 alternative:* Single-leg glute bridge, bodyweight. 3 × 10 each side.
*Tier 2 alternative:* Heavy loop band across hips.

---

**C1 — Lateral Band Walk**
*Hip abductor strength is critical for knee tracking in squats and lunges, pelvic stability during single-leg movements, and overall lower limb mechanics. The lateral band walk is a simple, effective way to load this pattern.*

Place a loop band just above the knees. Stand in a quarter-squat position, feet hip-width apart. Maintaining the squat position and keeping tension in the band throughout, step sideways 12 steps to the right, then 12 steps to the left. That is one set.

**Week 10:** 3 sets | Rest: 45 seconds | Band: Medium resistance

*Tier 1 alternative:* Side-lying hip abduction, 3 × 15 each side.

---

**C2 — Single-Leg Calf Raise**
*Often overlooked, calf strength is important for ankle stability, walking mechanics, and eventual return to impact activity. The single-leg variation also challenges balance.*

Stand on one foot, holding a wall lightly for balance if needed. Rise onto the toes slowly, hold for 1 second, then lower with control. Perform all reps on one side before switching.

**Week 10:** 3 × 12 each side | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 45 seconds

*Progression:* Hold a dumbbell in the same-side hand as the working leg once bodyweight is easy.

---

**Cool-Down (5 minutes)**
90-90 hip stretch (2 minutes each side), kneeling hip flexor stretch (90 seconds each side), supine spinal twist (1 minute each side), child's pose (2 minutes), diaphragmatic breathing to close (10 breaths).

---

### Day 2 — Upper Body Strength

**Warm-Up (5 minutes)**
Diaphragmatic breathing × 10, pelvic floor activation, cat-cow × 10, thoracic rotation seated × 10 each side, arm circles × 10 each direction, band pull-apart × 15 (or shoulder blade squeezes × 15).

---

**A1 — Dumbbell Row (Single Arm)**
*The single-arm row is the most important upper body exercise in this programme. Postpartum posture is dominated by anterior loading — rounded shoulders, protracted scapulae, forward head — from feeding, carrying, and sleep positions. Horizontal pulling directly counteracts this. It also strengthens the mid and upper back, which supports the spine under load in all other exercises.*

Place the left hand and left knee on the mat for support, right foot on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in the right hand, arm hanging straight down. On the exhale, drive the elbow toward the ceiling, retracting the shoulder blade at the top. The torso should not rotate. Lower slowly on the inhale.

**Week 10:** 3 × 10 each side | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 60 seconds | Load: 6–8kg | RPE: 6–7

*Tier 1 alternative:* Towel row — loop a towel around a door handle, lean back, and row the body toward the door. 3 × 12.
*Tier 2 alternative:* Resistance band anchored at waist height, single-arm row. 3 × 12.
*Cue:* "Lead with the elbow, not the hand." The arm is a hook — the back does the work.

---

**A2 — Dumbbell Floor Press**
*The floor press is the ideal introduction to loaded pressing for a postpartum client. The floor limits the range of motion, reducing shoulder stress, and the supine position means the abdominal wall is not loaded in the same way as a standing press. It is also safer than a bench press without a spotter.*

Lie on the back, knees bent, feet flat. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at chest height, elbows at approximately 45 degrees from the body — not flared out to 90 degrees. On the inhale, lower the elbows toward the floor until they touch lightly. On the exhale, press the dumbbells toward the ceiling until the arms are nearly straight.

**Week 10:** 3 × 10 | Tempo: 3-1-2-0 | Rest: 90 seconds | Load: 5–7kg each hand | RPE: 6

*Tier 1 alternative:* Incline push-up (hands on chair), 3 × 12. Progress to full push-up if able.
*Progression:* When floor press is strong and symptom-free, progress to a dumbbell bench press using a sturdy chair or low table as a bench, then eventually to a full bench press if gym access is available.

---

**B1 — Overhead Press (Seated or Standing)**
*The overhead press strengthens the shoulders, triceps, and upper back, and also challenges core stability as the load moves above the centre of gravity. Begin seated to reduce the demand on the core and pelvic floor, progressing to standing as stability improves.*

Sit cross-legged or on a chair with a neutral spine. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward. On the exhale, press the dumbbells overhead until the arms are nearly straight — do not lock the elbows. Lower slowly on the inhale.

**Week 10:** 3 × 10 | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 90 seconds | Load: 4–6kg each hand | RPE: 6

*Tier 1 alternative:* Seated shoulder press with water bottles or canned goods. 3 × 12.
*Progression trigger:* Move to standing overhead press when seated version is RPE 5 or below and pelvic floor is symptom-free under load.
*Watch for:* Excessive lower back arch during the press, which indicates the load is too heavy or the core is not adequately braced. Cue a gentle exhale and pelvic floor lift before each rep.

---

**B2 — Band Pull-Apart**
*This exercise directly targets the posterior deltoids, rhomboids, and mid-trapezius — the muscles most responsible for correcting the rounded-shoulder posture of new motherhood. It is simple, low-risk, and can be performed with a resistance band or even a towel.*

Hold a resistance band (or towel) with both hands at shoulder width, arms extended in front at shoulder height. On the exhale, pull the band apart by driving both hands outward and back, squeezing the shoulder blades together at the end range. Return slowly.

**Week 10:** 3 × 15 | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 45 seconds | Band: Light to medium

*Progression:* Increase band resistance, or perform face pulls by anchoring the band at face height and pulling toward the face with elbows high.

---

**C1 — Bicep Curl**
*Functional strength for carrying a baby, car seat, and pram. Also supports elbow and wrist health, which are frequently strained in new mothers due to repetitive carrying positions.*

Stand or sit with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing forward. On the exhale, curl both dumbbells toward the shoulders, keeping the elbows pinned to the sides. Lower slowly.

**Week 10:** 3 × 12 | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 45 seconds | Load: 4–6kg

---

**C2 — Tricep Kickback**
*Balances the bicep work and supports pushing movements. Also relevant for getting up from the floor — a movement performed dozens of times daily with a baby.*

Hinge forward from the hips to approximately 45 degrees, a dumbbell in each hand, upper arms pinned to the sides and parallel to the floor. On the exhale, extend the forearms back until the arms are straight. Lower slowly.

**Week 10:** 3 × 12 | Tempo: 2-1-3-0 | Rest: 45 seconds | Load: 3–5kg

---

**C3 — Forearm Plank (Full — Toes)**
*By Week 10, if the client has been symptom-free throughout Phase 3, progress from the knees-down plank to a full forearm plank. This is a significant milestone and should only be attempted if there is zero doming, zero pelvic floor symptoms, and the knees-down version is completely comfortable.*

Forearms on the mat, elbows under shoulders, toes on the mat, body in a straight line from heels to head. On the exhale, engage the pelvic floor and draw the lower belly gently in. Breathe normally — do not hold the breath. Hold for 20–30 seconds.

**Week 10:** 3 × 20–30 seconds | Rest: 60 seconds

*Regression:* If any doming, breath-holding, or pelvic floor symptoms occur, return to knees-down version immediately. There is no timeline pressure on this progression.
*Progression:* Build hold time to 45–60 seconds before adding any plank variations.

---

### Day 4 — Full Body Strength

**Theme:** Combine lower and upper body movements in supersets to increase metabolic demand and session efficiency. This mirrors real-life functional demands more closely than isolated sessions.

**Superset structure:** Perform exercise A1, rest 30 seconds, perform A2, rest 90 seconds, repeat for prescribed sets. This pairing of non-competing muscle groups allows one area to recover while the other works.

---

**Superset A — Squat and Row**

*A1 — Goblet Squat:* 3 × 10 | Load: Match or slightly exceed Week 10 Day 1 load | Tempo: 3-1-2-0

*A2 — Single-Arm Dumbbell Row:* 3 × 10 each side | Load: Match Day 2 load | Tempo: 2-1-3-0

Rest 90 seconds between supersets.

---

**Superset B — Hip Hinge and Press**

*B1 — Romanian Deadlift:* 3 × 10 | Load: Match or slightly exceed Day 1 load | Tempo: 3-1-2-1

*B2 — Floor Press or Incline Push-Up:* 3 × 10 | Load: Match Day 2 load | Tempo: 3-1-2-0

Rest 90 seconds between supersets.

---

**Superset C — Lunge and Pull**

*C1 — Reverse Lunge with Dumbbells:* 3 × 8 each leg | Load: Match Day 1 load | Tempo: 3-1-2-0

*C2 — Band Pull-Apart:* 3 × 15 | Tempo: 2-1-3-0

Rest 60 seconds between supersets.

---

**Finisher — Core and Carries**

*Farmer's Carry:*
This is one of the most functional and underrated exercises for a postpartum client. It directly mimics carrying a baby, shopping, or a car seat, and loads the entire body — grip, shoulders, core, pelvic floor, and legs — in an integrated way. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides. Stand tall with a neutral spine and engaged pelvic floor. Walk 10–15 metres, turn, and walk back. That is one length.

**Week 10:** 3 lengths | Load: 6–8kg each hand | Rest: 60 seconds between lengths

*Tier 1 alternative:* Carry two full water bottles or heavy bags of rice.
*Progression:* Increase load, distance, or introduce a suitcase carry (one side only) to challenge lateral core stability.

*Dead Bug:* 3 × 6 each side | Full extension | Slow and controlled.

**Theme:** Increase load by 1–2kg on all major compound movements where Week 10 felt like RPE 5–6. Introduce new exercise variations to increase stimulus. Add a fourth set to primary movements.

**Sumo Deadlift (from floor)**
*The sumo deadlift is introduced before the conventional deadlift because the wider stance and more upright torso reduce the demand on the lumbar extensors and anterior abdominal wall, making it more appropriate at this stage of recovery. It is also an excellent glute and inner thigh developer.*
